summary: Describes how 3270 display terminal data is transferred using existing Telnet capabilities, the practice traditionally called TN3270.

plainLanguage.summary: Old mainframes used special screens. TN3270 lets a regular computer act like one of those screens over the Internet.

questions: how does tn3270 work over telnet
which telnet options does tn3270 use
what are the 3270 attn and sysreq keys
subtitle: How IBM 3270 mainframe terminals were carried over ordinary Telnet connections, as practiced by vendors.

tldr.problem: IBM 3270 display terminals use block-mode data in EBCDIC, which differs from standard Telnet, yet IP users needed to reach existing IBM mainframes.
tldr.mechanism: TN3270 negotiates three existing Telnet options (Terminal-Type, Binary Transmission and End of Record) and then exchanges 3270 data streams, each ended with IAC EOR. SNA keys such as ATTN and SYSREQ are mapped onto existing Telnet commands.
tldr.outcome: The memo records what vendors already did and defines no new Telnet options or commands. RFC 1041 had tried to standardize this with a 3270 Regime option, but very few developers and vendors ever implemented it.

today: RFC 1576 is an Informational memo, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes practice as of January 1994 and notes that very few developers and vendors ever implemented the 3270 Regime option of RFC 1041.

sections.title: Why TN3270 Differs from Plain Telnet
sections.content:
3270 display terminal data is block mode and uses EBCDIC rather than ASCII. Those two differences are the main reason this memo separates TN3270 from standard Telnet.

Many vendors had introduced Telnet servers that give TCP/IP users a connection to existing IBM mainframes by supporting terminal emulation with a subset of Telnet. The server may sit on the host itself or connect to it by SNA or non-SNA methods. The memo documents this practice as it existed and says it also aims to help people build both servers and client emulators.
sections.plainLanguage: The old screens send a whole form at once, in a different alphabet from most computers. That is why they need their own special handling.

sections.title: Connection Negotiation
sections.content:
TN3270 defines no new Telnet options or commands. Clients connect to TCP port 23 and negotiate TERMINAL-TYPE (24), BINARY (0) and EOR (25), in any order. The client sends a terminal type string such as IBM-3278-2. The model suffix selects a screen size: -2 is 24x80, -3 is 32x80, -4 is 43x80 and -5 is 27x132. Adding -E means the terminal handles the 3270 extended data stream.

Before negotiating, some servers run a plain NVT dialog to collect a user name, a password or a destination host. They may negotiate ECHO so the client echoes locally. A server may also ask for SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD, and may try the 3270-REGIME option from RFC 1041, which the client can refuse with WONT.

If the server sends IAC WONT BINARY or IAC WONT EOR, the session no longer meets the TN3270 requirements and the client treats incoming data as NVT ASCII. The connection ends when either side closes the socket.
sections.plainLanguage: The two computers agree on a few ground rules first, like what kind of screen it is and how to tell where one message ends. After that they swap whole screens.

sections.title: Sending 3270 Data and Structured Fields
sections.content:
A 3270 data stream is a command plus its data, such as erase screen, erase and write, or read current screen. Since the commands carry no length, the EOR option separates them: each command and its data ends with IAC EOR. The Binary option is needed because 3270 data may contain the FF hexadecimal byte, which is the IAC character.

Structured fields allow features such as graphics, partitions and IPDS printer data streams. A client signals support by adding -E to the terminal type. The host can send a Read Partition Query and the client answers with a Query Reply listing the structured field functions it supports, which may be a null set.
sections.plainLanguage: Every screen is sent as one parcel with a special stamp at the end so the receiver knows where it stops.

sections.title: Keep-Alive, ATTN and SYSREQ
sections.content:
Servers test whether a client is still there with IAC NOP (hexadecimal F1), to which the client does not respond, or with the Timing Mark option, which the client refuses with WONT.

Two SNA keys are mapped to Telnet commands. A client sends the Telnet BREAK command (code 243) for the ATTN key, and the server passes it on as ATTN to the host application. For SYSREQ, which toggles between the application session and the SSCP session in SNA, clients send the Telnet Interrupt Process command or the 3270 Test Request key, depending on the server. Servers for non-SNA devices may ignore these. Support for both keys is not universal.
sections.plainLanguage: Special buttons on the old keyboard are turned into Telnet signals that travel over the Internet, and the server turns them back into button presses for the mainframe.

sections.title: What TN3270 Does Not Cover
sections.content:
The memo lists gaps. There is no way to emulate 328x printers, and a client cannot ask for a particular 3270 device name, which matters because many host applications behave differently depending on the terminal's network name. There is no SNA positive or negative response processing, which the memo says is part of what makes TN3270 efficient. Clients cannot get the SNA BIND information, and negotiation does not make clear whether clients should support structured fields.

Security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The list admits some things this setup cannot do, like pretending to be a printer or telling the host exactly which screen you are.
